I asked for the phone back because I felt like they were trying to establish dominance over Tj and trying to control him with cruel punishment and unfair rules, so I decided to take some of their “power” away by asking for my gift back.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action I took was morally acceptable or not. Let me start by understanding the situation clearly. So, I'm 21 years old, and I have two cousins, Tj who is 15 and Ked who is 13. When the new iPhones came out, I decided to gift each of them one. That was a nice gesture, right? I wanted them to have something special, especially since they're my cousins and I care about them. But then, Ked started stealing money from some extended family members. He admitted to it, which is good because it shows some level of responsibility, but the problem is his parents didn't seem to care. They defended him, didn't punish him, and even cut off the extended family members. That's where things started getting complicated. Over winter break, Ked apologized to the extended family and made amends. That's a positive step, but his parents are still stubborn and narcissistic. They refuse to admit they were wrong and now hate the extended family. That's a toxic environment for Ked to be in, especially since he's still a teenager. The extended family hosted a housewarming party and wanted all the cousins to spend the night. Both Tj and Ked wanted to come, but their parents told Ked he couldn't go in case the extended family tried accusing him of stealing again. They told Tj he could do whatever he wanted and trusted him to make the right decision. So, Ked stayed home, and Tj came to the sleepover. But then, Tj's phone started blowing up with his parents yelling at him for coming to the extended family's house. They were really upset, and it made Tj feel sad and disappointed. They trusted him to make the right decision, and he failed in their eyes. They also mentioned that if they hated someone, he had to hate them too. That's a lot of pressure for a 15-year-old. When Tj came back home, they grounded him and took his phone away for two weeks. Also, when Ked admitted to stealing, he never got punished. That's inconsistent and unfair. I can see why I'm upset about this. I told them that I can't control how they discipline their children, but it's not their property to take away from him. I won't go behind their backs and let him use the phone, but since it was my gift to him, I want to hold onto it until the two weeks are up. That makes sense because it's my property, and I have the right to decide what happens to it. But then, the narcissistic parents made a big deal out of it, and other extended family members are telling me I should have stayed out of it and let them raise their kid how they want. I'm only asking for the phone to be in my possession because I think they're treating him unfairly. We can all agree they're horrible parents. If they were decent parents and punishing him fairly, I wouldn't have asked for the phone back. Here's where I might be the asshole. I asked for the phone back because I felt like they were trying to establish dominance over Tj and trying to control him with cruel punishment and unfair rules. So, I decided to take some of their power away by asking for my gift back. Now, I need to evaluate whether this action is morally acceptable or not. Let's break it down. First, the phone was my gift to Tj. Legally and morally, it's my property, and I have the right to decide what happens to it. So, asking for it back is within my rights. However, by doing so, I'm interfering in how Tj's parents discipline him. Some people might argue that I should respect their authority as parents, even if I disagree with their methods. But in this case, their methods are inconsistent and unfair, which I find problematic. I also feel that by taking the phone back, I'm protecting Tj from their harmful influence. It's a way to stand up for him and show support, even if it means confronting his parents. On the other hand, some might see this as overstepping. I'm not their parent, and they have the right to discipline their child as they see fit, even if I don't agree with it. By taking the phone back, I'm inserting myself into their family dynamics, which could cause more conflict.
